big: Some investors own nine funds and cannot say what any of them is for. A simple core of one broad index fund, plus a little growth on top, can do the same job with less cost and less worry.

lines: I want something simple I can ignore for years.
Simple can still be well built. See the three parts of a core, how it drifts, and how cost builds up.

h: A core, a drift and a reset
alt: Three bars: the plan of sixty forty, the mix after a mid and small cap rally, and the mix after rebalancing
caps: The plan for ₹10 lakh: ₹6 lakh in one broad large cap index fund, ₹4 lakh in a mid and small cap fund.
A year later the large cap fund is up 10% and the mid and small cap fund 45%. The money is now ₹12.4 lakh.
The mix has drifted to about 53 and 47. That is nearly 7 points from the plan, past a 5 point trigger.
Rebalance: ₹7.4 lakh in the large cap fund, ₹5.0 lakh in the other. Back on plan. Returns are assumed.

h: Why cost matters in the core
alt: Bars comparing a portfolio with a cheap index core against an all active portfolio on yearly cost and value after 25 years
caps: Passive core: 60% in an index fund at 0.2%, 40% in an active fund at 1.2%. Blended cost is 0.6%.
All active at 1.2%. Cost per year on ₹10 lakh is ₹6,000 against ₹12,000.
Assume both earn 12% before costs. After 25 years: about ₹149 lakh against ₹130 lakh.
The difference is only cost. We still keep an active fund where a manager has room to add value.

h: Rules for a core you can ignore
title: Sound and unsound rules
stops: One broad index fund as the core
Rebalance when the mix drifts about 5 points
alt: A shield with sound and unsound rules for building a core with passive funds
caps: One broad index fund as the core. Add active only where a manager can add value after costs.
Keep the number of funds low, and review once a year.
Rebalance when the mix drifts well off plan, not on every small move.

q: Meena's plan is 60% in a large cap index fund and 40% in a mid and small cap fund, with a 5 point trigger. After a rally the mix is 53% and 47%. What should she do?
opts: Do nothing, since a mid cap rally means the plan is working
Rebalance, since the 7 point drift passes her trigger
Sell the mid and small cap fund entirely, since it grew too fast
Change the plan to 50 and 50, since mid caps are winning
why: The gain is welcome but the risk is now higher than she chose. The plan exists to keep that risk in check.
The mix is about 7 points off, past the 5 point trigger. Trim the winner, or steer new money to the large cap fund.
Selling all of it overshoots the plan. Rebalancing means returning to 60 and 40, not removing the growth part.
Chasing the winner raises risk at the point where it has just risen. Changing a plan after a rally is not rebalancing.

q: Rohan asks where a good active manager is most likely to beat the index after costs. What is the best answer?
opts: In large caps, where many analysts watch every share
Everywhere equally, since skill does not depend on segment
In less efficient areas, small caps more than large caps
Nowhere, since no active fund has ever beaten an index
why: Large caps are the most heavily studied, which is why many active funds there have struggled to beat the index.
Segments differ. Efficient markets leave little room, and less crowded ones leave more.
Small companies are followed by fewer analysts, so there is more room to find mispriced shares.
Some active funds do beat their index. The point is that it is harder in efficient segments.

q: A hands-off investor holds nine equity funds that overlap heavily and cannot recall why. What is the best first step?
opts: Add a tenth fund to cover segments that none of the nine hold
Keep all nine and ignore them, since checking only adds costs
Sell everything and wait for a better time to start again
Consolidate to an index core plus one or two growth funds
why: More funds add more clutter. The hands-off aim is a few funds with clear roles, not a bigger list.
Ignoring them keeps the overlap and cost. A yearly review is the minimum for any portfolio.
Selling everything is a timing bet and may bring tax. The task is to simplify, not to go to cash.
Fewer funds with clear jobs are easier to hold for years, cost less and avoid the overlap.

q: A core has 60% in an index fund charging 0.2% and 40% in an active fund charging 1.2%. What is the blended expense ratio?
opts: 0.6% a year, weighted by the money in each fund
0.7% a year, the simple average of the two rates
1.2% a year, since the active fund sets the cost
0.2% a year, since most of the money is in the index
why: 0.6 times 0.2 plus 0.4 times 1.2 is 0.12 plus 0.48, which is 0.6%. Each cost is weighted by its share.
The simple average counts both funds equally. But 60% of the money sits in the cheaper fund.
The active fund holds only 40% of the money, so the blend is well below its full rate of 1.2%.
Only 60% of the money sits in the cheaper fund. The other 40% costs 1.2%, so the blend is higher.

pts: Passive core plus a small active satellite, where a manager has room.
Rebalance once a year, or when the mix drifts about 5 points off plan.
Few funds, low cost. Simple is the plan you can actually keep.
